vignette: Ravi, an 18-year-old photographer from a South Eastern Asian background, had always harbored a passion for capturing the world through his lens. His life took a drastic turn when he was deployed overseas, where he experienced combat firsthand. The sights and sounds of war were imprinted deep within him, and he found himself unable to escape the vivid memories that now haunted his daily existence. Back home, the ordinary hum of life around him felt jarringly foreign, yet it was these sounds that would trigger those intense recollections of gunfire and chaos. Ravi couldn't pinpoint exactly when it started, but he knew he was trapped in a cycle of anxiety and agitation. Even in the safety of his own room, he could not relax; his body remained tense, anticipating danger that never arrived. He had come to believe that if he relaxed, he would somehow become vulnerable again, just as he had felt when bullets whizzed past him. The memories of his time in combat surged with an intensity far greater than any recollection of ordinary events. Each time these memories replayed in his mind, they reinforced his negative appraisals, leading him to believe that he was unworthy of happiness and that his survival was a mark of failure. Ravi often felt as if those moments replayed in high-definition, more vivid than any mundane experience he had ever known. Each time the memories surged, they echoed back to him, reinforcing his belief that he was unworthy of happiness and fundamentally flawed, feeding into a deep-seated conviction that he was somehow broken. Each time these memories invaded his thoughts, they reinforced his negative beliefs about himself, leading him to feel that he was unworthy of happiness and fundamentally flawed. This clarity was both a gift and a curse; each time he recalled the faces of his fallen comrades, a wave of rage washed over him. He would picture their smiles and laughter, only to be engulfed by the guilt of having survived when they had not. It was a bitter reminder of his perceived failures, and he often thought that he should have done more to protect them. This sense of inadequacy compounded his feelings of mistrust towards others; he felt that no one could understand his pain, and consequently, he began to withdraw from relationships. His ongoing belief that he had failed his comrades made it difficult for him to trust anyone; he feared that if he let others in, they would see the same weaknesses he saw in himself. This belief in his unworthiness created a lens through which every new situation felt fraught with potential danger, making him hyper-aware of his vulnerabilities and convinced that he was always at risk of failing again. Ravi felt he belonged nowhere, as if the war had stripped him of his place in the world. The persistent sense of threat that enveloped him contributed to this feeling, as he couldn't shake the idea that if he was always in danger, it meant he was inherently flawed, unable to protect himself or those he cared about. This persistent sense of isolation only intensified his feelings of vulnerability, leading him to believe that danger was always lurking just beyond his reach. This constant sense of threat made the memories of combat more vivid, as if the adrenaline of feeling endangered pulled those painful recollections closer to the surface, demanding his attention. The more he felt this persistent sense of threat, the more those memories invaded his mind, as though he needed to keep reliving them to brace himself against the danger he believed was always looming. The persistent feeling of danger kept Ravi's traumatic memories alive, as he felt compelled to revisit those harrowing experiences, believing they would help him stay vigilant against threats. In moments of heightened stress, the memories would flood back, as if the threat itself pulled them from the depths of his mind, reminding him of the chaos he had lived through and the failures he could not escape. The memories of combat were also inextricably linked to his current state of being. Each recollection reinforced his belief that he had failed to protect his comrades, which in turn deepened his feelings of worthlessness and despair. Whenever he recalled those harrowing moments, he was immediately thrown back into that place of despair, where the weight of responsibility and loss bore down on him. The profound guilt of surviving when others did not only reinforced his negative self-image, leading him to believe that he was fundamentally flawed and undeserving of happiness. The ongoing threat he felt confirmed his deepest fears, whispering to him that he was not the kind of person who could be safe, further entrenching his negative beliefs about himself. His mind would spiral into a vortex of negative thoughts, reinforcing the belief that he had failed to protect his comrades. This cycle of negative appraisal made Ravi feel threatened by the world around him; he began to see every corner and shadow as a potential source of danger, a reminder of his past failures. The more he reflected on these memories, the more isolated he felt, as if they had created an insurmountable barrier between him and the people around him. This constant cycle of reflection, fuelled by his negative appraisals, made the memories more vivid, each time adding weight to his belief that he was unworthy of connection and belonging. Each recollection brought with it a fresh wave of anger, not only at the circumstances but at himself for not being able to prevent the outcome. This cycle of memory and negative appraisal left him feeling trapped, with no way out. In his day-to-day life as a photographer, Ravi noticed that certain sounds-a car backfiring, a door slamming-would catch him off guard, forcing him to jump as if under attack. These ordinary sounds, which should have been benign, acted as haunting reminders of the chaos he had endured. The constant threat he felt from these triggers kept his traumatic memories alive, compelling him to revisit the horrors of combat in an effort to stay alert to potential danger. Every time he felt that sense of impending danger, the memories surged forth - as if his body was reminding him of the chaos he had experienced, reinforcing the belief that he could never let his guard down. He often found himself engaging in risky behaviors, almost as if he were trying to provoke danger, believing it was the only way to regain control over his life. Despite the inherent risks, the adrenaline high felt like a temporary escape from the emotional turmoil he could not shake. Yet, each time he took a risk, he only deepened the chasm of his negative beliefs, feeling as though he was proving his own unworthiness. His negative appraisals of himself led to a pervasive sense of threat; he walked through life convinced that danger lurked around every corner, reflecting his belief that he was inherently vulnerable. Now, as he sat in the therapist's office, Ravi felt a mix of apprehension and hope. He had finally reached a point where he could no longer manage the weight of his experiences alone. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never feel whole again, that he would remain trapped in this cycle of pain and mistrust. This ongoing sense of threat confirmed his deepest fears-that he was fundamentally broken and unworthy of safety and connection. The persistent sense of threat led him to believe that he was perpetually vulnerable, confirming his fears that he was not equipped to protect himself or those he cared about. Yet, beneath that fear, there was a glimmer of hope; he hoped to reconnect with the world, to find a way to process his memories without being consumed by them. Ravi yearned for a path forward, one where he could reclaim his life and his passion for photography, free from the shadows of his past.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not establish that negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat for Ravi.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."

  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."

  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."

  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
